RELIGION CORNER Starting a Conversation By Pastor Jim Hopkins Though there were other roads he could have taken, Jesus chose to pass through Samaria on his way to the Galilee in order to start a conversation with a Samaritan woman. He met her at Jacob’s well. Though there was significant enmity between observant Jews, like Jesus, and the Samaritans, Jesus thought it was time to build some bridges. Stopping at the storied well, Jesus asked a woman who had come to draw water for a drink. This request started a conversation about spiritual thirst, living water, true worship, the woman’s life and connections between groups that didn’t want to admit that they had much in common. The woman is an active participant in the conversation and, when she identifies Jesus as a prophet, he does what prophets do, he speaks important truth. In this case he makes it clear that the spiritual destinies of the Samaritan people and the Jewish people are intertwined and promises that, together, they will worship the One God in “spirit and in truth.” He started a conversation to lift up a vision of shared worship, shared values, shared truth and shared hope. In a similar fashion a follower of Jesus, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., attempted to start a conversation with the American people about our common destiny, race and racial justice. As early as 1962 this American prophet was saying, “We must learn to live together as brothers or we will perish together as fools.” Some in the United States were, like the woman at the well, willing participants in the conversation. Many were not. Many are still not. Central to this conversation were Dr. King’s beliefs that: • There was a great need to abolish the idea of superior and inferior races • Though laws don’t change people’s hearts, they were still need to regulate their actions • That the American dream is the dream that all can live together The vision Jesus shared with the woman at the well for their time, is startlingly similar to the vision Dr. King lifted for his time. articles.text: No public process seen in city’s plans for development of lots Editor: Through this letter, I am reaching out to all fellow Piedmont residents who may not yet fully understand what our City leaders intend to do to our neighborhoods – without advance notice to us and without giving us an opportunity to be heard. Attached below is a listing of vacant, single-family residential lots in Piedmont, as reported by the City Council in its “6th Cycle Housing Element” plan. These lots are next door to many of us, or perhaps right down the street or just around the corner. They are appropriately zoned for single-family homes. The City Council and its Planning Department, however, want each and every one of these lots to be developed with up to four homes per lot. The City has seized upon a controversial state law, known as “SB 9,” as the vehicle by which developers are being invited in to split and rapidly build out these lots with multiple family dwellings – via a rubber-stamped, “ministerial” approval process that is intentionally designed to not tell us what is happening until it is too late. Don’t take my word for it. Just drop by 77 Wistaria Way (one of some 60 lots on the City’s hit list) and view the concrete monstrosity being erected there. The developer is shoehorning three dwelling units into a steep, treacherous lot that until now had been a wooded sanctuary with a creek running through it. A creek that the City itself promised to preserve. Instead of following normal design and building code public review for a single-family home, this multiple family development was allowed to bypass all those requirements and was blessed by junior Planning staff, without Planning Commission or City Council consideration. And without timely notice to neighbors, or any fair opportunity for neighbors to raise important safety and environmental issues. This despite the fact that even SB 9 does not prohibit the City from affording residents this modicum of fairness. Snap a few pix if you wish and take the Wistaria Way image with you and then look at the addresses on the City’s hit list, shown below. See any location there near your home? (How about you folks on Howard and Nace Avenues?) Then ask yourself: Do I think that having multiple family units built there without public notice or comment reflects the level of respect for residents I expect from my City leaders? I have asked the City Council and the City Attorney at the very least to provide minimal notice and opportunity for residents to be heard whenever an SB 9 multi-family lot split and development application is filed. But even this modest request has been met repeatedly with stony silence. Maybe when more of us end up with this in our own backyards, enough voices will be heard to make a difference. But please, don’t wait to see something to do something. By then it will be too late. Respectfully, Harvey L. articles.text: Editor: A headline on the front page of the December 11, 2024, Piedmont Post incorrectly states that the new community pool project has a cost overrun of 79 percent. This is misleading and erroneous. The Post arrives at this number by using the $19.5 million face value of the Measure UU bond measure as the basis for computing the cost overrun percentage. It is more appropriate to use the December 5, 2022, City Council approved project budget of $28.9 million as the basis, resulting in a 20% cost overrun – not 79%. We, the members of the Measure UU Pool Bond Oversight Committee, have been meeting regularly since October 13, 2022, and have carefully followed spending for the Piedmont Community Pool Project. We believe that it is important to correct the record. Here are the facts. 1. The total pool project cost was estimated at $23 million on July 20, 2020, with a recommended face value amount of $19.5 million in bonds to be issued. The actual net proceeds of the $19.5 million bond measure came in at $24.4 million because they were sold at a premium. 2. The City Council approved a total project budget of $28.9 million on December 5, 2022, when it awarded the construction contract. This includes both hard costs (construction) and soft costs (project management, architectural design, engineering). A major contributor to the increased budget was the unprecedented 32% spike in the California construction cost index from July 2020 (initial pool cost estimate) to January 2023 when construction began. 3. The City Council has approved three subsequent increases to the pool project, bringing the total budget to $34.9 million. These increases have been due to weather related project delays, utilities and undergrounding requirements, the discovery of two buried fuel tanks at the site, remediation costs, soil disposal, the complexity of pool electrification, and other factors.
articles.title: Setting the record straight on pool cost overrun

articles.text: Editor: There is a 4-unit duplex project with a 4-car garage in two 30-foot high structures proposed for 210 Howard Avenue under SB 9. It is a very different animal than 77 Wisteria Lane. The Wisteria neighborhood tried to stop the project based on CEQA concerns. Our concern is about safety and possible serious injury to kids going down the sidewalk to Beach School, going alone or running ahead of their parents. In normal times, prior to the advent of SB 9, a similar project would have been shut down from the get-go. But SB 9 will allow someone to walk a 4-unit condominium, 4-car garage project through a City with a very rushed, expedited review process with no public hearings or review. SB 9 is going to change Piedmont forever and there’s very little a resident can do. This is a very dangerous, small flag lot with a very long flagpole/driveway that doesn’t meet Piedmont standards for width and exiting sight lines/visibility and has cross slopes that exceed 20% as one would move down the driveway. This is misleading and erroneous. The Post arrives at this number by using the $19.5 million face value of the Measure UU bond measure as the basis for computing the cost overrun percentage. It is more appropriate to use the December 5, 2022, City Council approved project budget of $28.9 million as the basis, resulting in a 20% cost overrun – not 79%. We, the members of the Measure UU Pool Bond Oversight Committee, have been meeting regularly since October 13, 2022, and have carefully followed spending for the Piedmont Community Pool Project. We believe that it is important to correct the record. Here are the facts. 1. The total pool project cost was estimated at $23 million on July 20, 2020, with a recommended face value amount of $19.5 million in bonds to be issued. The actual net proceeds of the $19.5 million bond measure came in at $24.4 million because they were sold at a premium. 2. The City Council approved a total project budget of $28.9 million on December 5, 2022, when it awarded the construction contract. This includes both hard costs (construction) and soft costs (project management, architectural design, engineering). A major contributor to the increased budget was the unprecedented 32% spike in the California construction cost index from July 2020 (initial pool cost estimate) to January 2023 when construction began. 3. The City Council has approved three subsequent increases to the pool project, bringing the total budget to $34.9 million. These increases have been due to weather related project delays, utilities and undergrounding requirements, the discovery of two buried fuel tanks at the site, remediation costs, soil disposal, the complexity of pool electrification, and other factors. It should also be noted that the total pool project costs are funded by not only the Measure UU bond measure, but also included PRFO, PBF, Kroeger Estate, grants, a zero-interest rate loan for pool electrification, and the sewer and facilities capital funds. In summary, the $19.5 million face value for Measure UU was never intended to represent the total cost for building a new community pool, nor does it represent the actual funding Measure UU bonds provided for the project. When computing the cost overrun, the appropriate baseline is $28.9 million, the total project budget approved by City Council before construction began. This equates to a 20% cost overrun – not 79% as reported by the Piedmont Post. articles.text: Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan will deliver a presentation on wildfire readiness in Piedmont at the Public Safety Committee meeting in City Hall on Thursday, January 23, at 5:30 p.m. Community members are encouraged to attend and speak at the meeting in person. Video of the presentation will be available for viewing afterwards on the City’s website. Chief Brannigan will describe the City of Piedmont’s work to prepare for, respond to, and mitigate risk from wildfires, including both City-specific initiatives and collaborative regional work. The presentation will discuss the ongoing wildfires in Los Angeles, the risks a similar event could pose to Piedmont, and two Fire Department initiatives currently in progress that aim to address these risks – an update of the City’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan and a community wildfire evacuation exercise planned for May 2025. The Local Hazard Mitigation Plan update, which began last fall, is a data-driven process to develop a roadmap for actions the City can take now that could prevent or reduce potential impacts of a wildfire or other disaster, such as: • creating programs to help residents make their properties more resilient • strengthening building codes • retrofitting/rebuilding critical infrastructure and facilities Documenting these projects in a formally adopted mitigation plan will position Piedmont to apply for state and federal disaster assistance and mitigation grants. The wildfire evacuation exercise allows the City to test organization-wide emergency response protocols and identify any gaps in procedures or training, while also providing community members a practical opportunity to test their own household’s preparation. Community participation is critical to the success of both efforts. The presentation will highlight upcoming opportunities to get involved, including a public workshop scheduled for Wednesday, March 26, where participants will collaborate to brainstorm and prioritize mitigation projects or programs. Visit piedmont.ca.gov/LHMP to learn more about the Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, sign up for email updates, and provide input to the project team. Visit piedmont.ca.gov/disaster for information on preparing your household for wildfires and other disasters, including creating an evacuation plan, packing a go-bag, and managing vegetation to reduce risk on your property. articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC) has been awarded a $20,000 grant by the National Endowment for the Arts for its project Echoes of Eureka, a mostly textless choral opera focused on the experiences of Chinese citizens during the Expulsion Acts in the 19th century. The opera, composed by Piedmont Choirs Artistic Director Eric Tuan, will premiere as a part of the choir’s Making History Concert on April 12. It will also be performed at a festival in Eureka in Northern California in early May. Established by Congress in 1965, the NEA is an independent federal agency and one of the largest funders of the arts and arts education in communities nationwide. The NEA has awarded over 1,400 grants nationwide, totaling more than $36 million in funds as part of their recent announcement of fiscal year 2025 grants. “Connecting to the HAPI community in Eureka, Eric is building a powerful new work that will spark conversations,” wrote Executive Director Keri Butkevich in the PEBCC newsletter. “This grant supports not only the premiere and Eureka tour performance in May 2025, but also the fostering of new outreach relationships within the AAPI community throughout the Bay Area.” Aligning with focus on accessibility, the grant provides for ASL and translation materials for the work’s premiere at PEBCC’s Making History concert this spring. Tuan has been working closely with the Asian and Pacific Islander communities in Eureka and Humboldt County to create his work. Echoes of Eureka will begin with an acknowledgement for the families and individuals that were affected by the Chinese Expulsion in the late 1800s. “It’s an important story that needs to be told. And we’re very honored to be able to bring this work to life through the support and the recognition by our peers at the national level at the NEA,” said Butkevich. “I believe it’s one of the first awards that we’ve been granted for a project that was outside of our school,” she added. “It means a lot to see the expanded support. I think it honors the legacy of the core families in Piedmont that started the choir. And I think it also leads to the expanded impact that the choir has, reaching over 23 communities and singers from over 90 schools across the Bay Area.” Sue Malick, a former board member and longtime supporter of Piedmont Choirs, said, “Piedmont is so fortunate to have the treasures that the choir brings to our community and the world.” The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choi

The event began with opening remarks by PADC President Ellen Lee and Event Founder Lois Corrin, followed by an Acknowledgement of Native land by Jean Takazawa, Director of Diversity for Piedmont Unified School District. Piedmont Mayor Betsy Andersen addressed the audience after the opening, speaking about Piedmont’s fight against racism and exclusion, including the City’s plans to create a memorial to Sydney and Irene Dearing. “Dr. King knew that change doesn’t happen within our comfort zones,” said Andersen. “It happens when we are willing to listen, to learn, and to push forward together. That is why events like today matter.” Congresswomen Lateefah Simon offered much to think about in her speech on peace, responsibility, and accountability in the upcoming days of administration at the national level. Her message to keep moving and keep “fighting against the oppressions that will come” seems more pertinent than ever, especially after reports of tech billionaire Elon Musk performing a Nazi salute after the presidential inauguration later that same day. “We’re supposed to talk about joy and love today, but King was a serious man and he said consistently that he was about His Father’s business,” said Simon. “We will keep moving. I understand the charge,” said Simon. “The dream is big but we will get there.” Piedmont High School student Hunter Fastau, co-President of the African Affinity Student Union, introduced the keynote speaker, Ericka Huggins, before Fastau sat down for a “fireside chat” with the lifelong activist. Huggins spoke about her experience as an educator and activist, her husband’s assassination and her subsequent incarceration by the FBI, and the role of young people in social activism. “Please know that the underpinning of social justice is serving humanity with love,” advised Huggins. History is a river. And what I think, or feel, about Martin Luther King is that he showed us how to step into that river,” said Huggins. The 4th annual Art & Writing Showcase presented youth works created for MLK Day as a slide show. Destiny Arts Dance Company and the Oakland Youth Chorus singers both held performances between the speeches. Destiny Arts mixed dance and spoken-word poetry as they struck powerful ensemble poses throughout their routines. The Oakland Youth Chorus sang songs of light and togetherness which got the audience standing and singing along to their final song of the night, “Lift Every Voice and Sing” by James Weldon Johnson. Piedmont Students Samuel Bahala and Naylah Kasaun of the PHS African Affinity Student Union addressed the audience before the closing song with a call to action. “Let’s stand up and show the world that we’re more than the colors and negative descriptions that are seen, because I believe in each of us are deep stories that can shine,” said Bahala reading from a poem titled “Until When?” “Let the world see us not as our limits, but as a bright light. For in the diversity of who we are, we shine strong and bright like diamonds.” Students Samuel Bahala (left) and Naylah Kasaun of the African Affinity Student Union give a Call to Action before the last performance. articles.text: To support Highlander Robotics’ goal of encouraging girls and women in STEM, this year’s outreach program was expanded to Girl Scouts by hosting two new workshops. Brownies and Cadettes both learned about robotics and engineering in the PHS Makers Fab Lab at PHS, an experience that also earned the girls their requirements for engineering badges. The first workshop, held in early November for Brownies aged seven to nine, was based around building a spring bot using basic principles of physics and energy. After a short presentation by 8033 members Cassie Colby, Tristen Milsum, Athena Li, and Lewy Seiden, the younger scouts got to build and test their own designs. Experimenting with different variables and recording the results is key to problem solving, just as a real scientist or engineer would. Brownies test out their spring bot and record the results while earning their Engineering Badges. The second workshop, geared for older middle school Cadette scouts, went deeper into the design process of robotics, challenging them to design and build their own catapults. They also had a brief lesson about the science behind catapults and the engineering process. Each group got to design and build their own catapults, and then also had the opportunity to tour the robotics lab for a closer look at Team 8033’s Crescendo robot. Brownies and Cadettes both learned about robotics and engineering in the PHS Makers Fab Lab at PHS, an experience that also earned the girls their requirements for engineering badges. The first workshop, held in early November for Brownies aged seven to nine, was based around building a spring bot using basic principles of physics and energy. After a short presentation by 8033 members Cassie Colby, Tristen Milsum, Athena Li, and Lewy Seiden, the younger scouts got to build and test their own designs. Experimenting with different variables and recording the results is key to problem solving, just as a real scientist or engineer would. Brownies test out their spring bot and record the results while earning their Engineering Badges. The second workshop, geared for older middle school Cadette scouts, went deeper into the design process of robotics, challenging them to design and build their own catapults. They also had a brief lesson about the science behind catapults and the engineering process. Each group got to design and build their own catapults, and then also had the opportunity to tour the robotics lab for a closer look at Team 8033’s Crescendo robot. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. articles.text: Piedmont head coach Ben Spencer achieved his 100th win at Piedmont in a game with Terra Linda on January 18. Pictured are Beach Lorin (left), Nicholas Riordan, Johnny Lee, Dillon Casey, Cash Panico (back), Lucian Fang-Ring, assistant coach Jason Harris, head coach Ben Spencer, assistant coach Kalen Davison (back), assistant coach Shamaree Worley, Emmet Asulin (back), Akash Bornstein, P.J. Brayer, and Ravi Silverberg. Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team finished up a busy week with four games. The 61-54 victory over Terra Linda on Saturday, January 18 marked a milestone for PHS coach Ben Spencer. It was the team’s100th win since he became the head coach. “It came faster than I expected,” Spencer said. “It’s nice to get it off your back but we’re just focusing on the next game. It’s a small goal, but it’s about winning NCS, league, and State. It’s exciting to get to 100 and I’ve been lucky to have great players,” Spencer said. Spencer and his assistant coaches Shamaree Worley and Jason Harris took over the varsity squad in the winter of 2019-20, and led the school to the Division 4 North Coast Section championship, the school’s first section title. They also reached last year’s NCS Finals as a Div.3 team.. “I think we’ve gotten a lot better at teaching. We were privileged early on with that NCS team that had nine seniors. That year, we could just roll the ball out. The last few years, we had good players and teams, but the talent wasn’t as great as that NCS year. With our strength of schedule, we’ve focused on the fundamentals. I think that’s been the biggest thing toward building tough and smart basketball players,” Spencer said. The Highlanders had a pair of Western Alameda County Conference losses over the past week, 78-53 to Bishop O’Dowd at home on Tuesday, January 13, and 65-51 to Berkeley two days later. PHS battled to a 73-64 loss to Branson at the MLK Showcase at Merritt College on Monday, January 20. In each of the games, PHS fell behind early and couldn’t recover. “It’s been our Achilles heel with the young team, we come out slow when we’re just as good or better than the team we’re competing against. Berkeley, they started with an 11-0 run. Bishop O’Dowd went on a 12-nothing run to start the second half. Terra Linda started off 11-3 and today we started 11-0. We’re spotting teams points and we’re not coming out ready to play. It’s frustrating, but the fight is there,” Spencer said. 73-64 to Branson Branson came out hot with an 11-0 lead and carried a 24-14 lead through the first quarter. In the second, Piedmont clawed back to a 26-24 deficit, but the Bulls carried a 34-29 lead into halftime. Branson carried a nine-point 52-43 lead into the fourth, but Piedmont was able to cut it close in the final going. In the late minutes of the fourth, Piedmont cut the deficit to just three points when Lucian Fang-Ring found Ravi Silverberg for a 3-pointer to make it 64-61, but that’s the closest things got with the Bulls going on a seven point run to pull ahead by 10, 71-61. Final scorers: Silverberg led with 22 points, Casey had 16, Fang-Ring had nine, Cash Panico had eight, P.J. Brayer had seven, and Beach Lorin had two. Staff Photos Ravi Silverberg led the scoring against Branson and Terra Linda. Dillon Casey had 16 points against Branson, 14 against Terra Linda, and 16 against Berkeley.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team wrapped up a rough week, winning one of their last three games to bring its record to 13-3. They lost to Western Alameda County Conference rival Bishop O’Dowd 56-47 at home on Tuesday, January 14, defeated Menlo School 52-33 on Saturday, January 18 in the MLK Shootout at St. Mary’s of Stockton, and lost 81-66 to Centennial of Las Vegas at the MLK Classic at Bishop O’Dowd on Monday, January 20. Their loss to the Centennial Bulldogs came against a topthree rated team in Nevada, and a team expected to compete for its state title. They possessed several players over 6-feet tall. “They were a good team and aggressive. If we fell asleep for one second, they would make you pay. We shot decently but then we let them off the hook. They are ranked as one of the best teams in Nevada. We just have to find a way to compete longer,” coach Bryan Gardere said. 81-66 loss to Centennial The two sides battled to an 18-18 tie through the first quarter, while Centennial carried a narrow 40-37 lead into halftime. Piedmont cut the deficit to 59-57 to start the fourth quarter, but the Bulldogs height and athleticism was too much for the Highlanders in the final going—getting outscored 22-10 in the fourth. Piedmont held a lead late in the third quarter after Jenelle Solis found Andrea Martin for a 3-pointer to take a 54-53 lead with 1:43 left, but it was the last time PHS held an advantage. Centennial took a 55-54 lead with 1:07 left and never relinquished. Centennial forward Nation Williams, listed at 6 feet, 2 inches, led the Bulldogs with 24 points. and 6-foot guard D’Arrah Mitchell added 22 points. Final stats: Briana Webb led scoring with 22 points and seven rebounds. Martin scored 10 points, seven rebounds, three assists, and one block. Savannah Dennig had five points, four rebounds, three assists, and one steal. Solis scored 10 points, six assists, and two steals. Shakila Zuberi had nine points, one rebound and assist. Taylor White scored seven points, five rebounds, two assists, two steals, and a block. Cleo Afsar had three rebounds and three assists. 52-33 win vs. Menlo School Piedmont led 18-6 through the first quarter, but only scored seven points in the second quarter to cling onto a 25-22 lead at halftime. PHS turned up the intensity in the second half, outscoring Menlo School 17-6 in the third to lead 42-28, then added 10 more points in the fourth and only allowed five. Final stats: Martin scored 15 points, six rebounds, three assist, and four blocks. Dennig had two points, nine rebounds, and one assist. Solis had nine points, four rebounds, five assists, and a steal. Zuberi had two points, six rebounds, and one assist. White scored six points, six rebounds, four assists, two steals, and two blocks. Webb had seven points and nine rebounds. Afsar had nine points and three rebounds. Saniyah Johnson had two points, two rebounds, two steals, and one block. Staff Photos Briana Webb led the scoring against Centennial with 22 points. Andrea Martin had 10 points against Centennial, 15 vs. Menlo School, and eight points against O’Dowd.

articles.text: Piedmont tied San Leandro 1-1 and fell 2-0 to Berkeley. Staff Photos The Highlander boys’ soccer team had mixed results in games last week. They lost 2-0 to Berkeley at Witter Field on Friday, January 17 and drew 1-1 with San Leandro at Burrell Field two days earlier. The team is still searching for its first win against league competition. Coach Ben Russell is hoping the team can establish its attacking fluidity. “Berkeley has good quality and has a big talent pool. But it was good to see the boys’ motivation. We competed and had little moments where things could’ve boiled over. Defensively, just one little lapse against teams with good quality can hurt us. We haven’t been able to build our offensive structure into the game just yet. Hopefully we can continue this competitive mindset into the next game and avoid dropping quality,” Russell said following the loss to Berkeley. articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet premiere of Sir Kenneth MacMillan’s Manon opens the company’s 2024/25 Repertory Season this Friday, January 24. Inspired by the 1731 novel Manon Lescaut by Abbé Prévost, Manon is considered one of MacMillan’s most notable and widely-celebrated works. The ballet chronicles the rise and fall of its titular heroine, beginning near Paris and ending in New Orleans. The three-act ballet was first performed by The Royal Ballet in London in 1974 with Antoinette Sibley and Anthony Dowell in principal roles. “MacMillan was an artist who infused novelty and depth into his choreography,” San Francisco Ballet Artistic Director Tamara Rojo said. “Manon exemplifies how he brought new life to a classic story, transforming it into a timeless narrative.” Principal casting for Manon includes Dores André, Jasmine Jimison, Sasha De Sola, and Nikisha Fogo as Manon. The principal dancers also include Harrison James, Max Cauthorn, and Aaron Robison as des Grieux. San Francisco Ballet welcomes principal guest artist Alban Lendorf to the War Memorial Opera House stage for select performances as des Grieux. The War Memorial Opera House bars will serve a specialty cocktail inspired by the themes of Manon and 18th-century France. Manon is performed on stage through February 1. articles.text: Speaker event at museum also live-streamed Feb. 1 Curators at the de Young Museum will host a discussion on the iconic artist Tamara de Lempicka and how she used fashion as a way to craft her own artistic identity. The retrospective Tamara de Lempicka, the first exhibition in the United States dedicated to the artist’s full oeuvre, includes more than 150 works on view as well as a number of rarely seen drawings and still lifes. “Considering San Francisco’s history as a great Art Deco capital of the world, the exhibition, aptly presented in close proximity to landmarks of the period such as the Golden Gate Bridge and Coit Tower, adds to our understanding not only of Lempicka’s work specifically, but also this influential art and design period at large,” said Thomas Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. Artwork from Lempicka’s early Parisian years feature melancholic interiors and a selection of Art Deco objects, sculptures and dresses from the Fine Arts Museums’ permanent collection. Through her world-renowned paintings, Lempicka celebrated the changing world of women’s fashion in the 1920s and 1930s. Patrons view the retrospective Tamara de Lempicka exhibit at de Young Museum. The artist also wore designs by contemporary fashion powerhouses like Jean Patou and Marcel Rochas, and used fashion to craft her own artistic and public identity. The speaker event will be at 1 p.m. on February 1 in the museum’s Koret Auditorium and is free to ticket-holders. Seating is first-come, first-served. The discussion will also be live-streamed at the same time and is free on the museum’s website. The discussion will be led by museum curators Furio Rinaldi, the Lempicka exhibition co-curator, and Laura Camerlengo, the fine arts museum’s textile and costume expert. “Lempicka’s drawings reveal both the artist’s outstanding technical refinement as a designer and her breath of visual sources,” said Rinaldi. “The core of her unique style [draws] from Italian Mannerism to the French Neoclassicism, the Russian avant-garde and the innovative graphic language of fashion illustrators like George Barbier, Helen Dryden and Georges Lepape.” Camerlengo is curator in charge of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, and since 2010, has organized and presented numerous costume and textile exhibitions for the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco and the Philadelphia Museum of Art. To learn more, visit https:// www.famsf.org/events/conversation-lempicka-fashion.

Attendees will learn about the fascinating and colorful traditions of Lunar New Year, celebrated by various Asian cultures, including the symbolism behind lanterns, firecrackers, red envelopes, and traditional food. Kids will enjoy learning how to Lion Dance and play with handmade rattle drums. Park visitors are encouraged to wear red this weekend for good luck. Han first discovered jazz in high school when she heard “Chance” by Kenny Kirkland from his album and decided to pursue the genre in her own musical career. Her album Crime Zone seized the attention of the jazz world and established herself as a fast-rising star on the scene. Her follow-up, Iron Starlet, also gained critical acclaim. articles.text: Qi Baishi: Inspiration In Ink, an exhibition celebrating the life and work of renowned Chinese ink painter Qi Baishi, is now on view at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. The exhibition marks the 160th anniversary of Baishi’s birth and features 42 works on paper on loan from the Beijing Fine Art Academy, where he served as the academy’s first honorary director. Inspiration In Ink is the first time many of the displayed works have been presented in the United States. “Qi Baishi’s long and storied life witnessed China’s dramatic passage from the Qing Dynasty to the new republic period and the rise of socialism,” said Fan Jeremy Zhang, Asian Art Museum’s Curator of Chinese Art. “Renowned as the people’s artist, Qi declined to enjoy retirement. Instead, he tirelessly explored ink art in his later years, aiming to share his love of nature among a wide audience and help them find enlightenment in everyday life.” Zhang added that the artist’s “technical abilities and expressionistic approach imbue his art with a spiritual quality, inviting viewers to contemplate the deeper significance of everyday motifs.” “His work resonates so widely with audiences because he not only captures his subjects but also seeks to express their spirit through calligraphic, spontaneous strokes, something that requires master brushwork,” Zhang said. In 1960, Baishi became the first Chinese artist to have a solo exhibition at the de Young Museum in San Francisco. Although he has humble roots, his pieces have achieved record-breaking prices at auctions worldwide, with his “Twelve Landscape Screens” (1925) selling for a $141 million in 2017. “His ability to capture the beauty in the ordinary contributed to his growing popularity inside and outside of China, a legacy that continues to thrive today,” said Rob Mintz, Chief Curator at the Asian Art Museum. “Qi Baishi’s quotidian subject matter and whimsical, playful style made his art incredibly accessible to audiences at the time, making him the first Chinese painter to capture the attention of American audiences,” Mintz added. The exhibition will be on view through April. Visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/exhibitions/ qi-baishi-inspiration-in-ink/ to learn more and to purchase museum tickets. Set in Nazi occupied France during WWII, White Bird is a compelling story of courage and kindness. The story authored by R.J. Palacio is considered to be thematically connected to the author’s first book and film, Wonder. The film opens in the present with a middle school boy Julian (Bryce Gheisar) coming home from school to what he thinks is an empty house. Instead he is surprised by his grandmother, Sara (Helen Mirren), who tells him that she is aware of his expulsion from his previous school for bullying a classmate. She asks him to sit down in the dining room and tells him a story that takes place during the Nazi occupation of France in World War II. And so her narrative begins. Sara (Ariella Glaser), a young Jewish girl on the cusp of adolescence, is counseled by her parents regarding the possible dangers for Jews. She barely grasps the full significance of the Nazi’s presence in their town. One of her classmates is Julien, his right leg crippled by childhood polio, and therefore walks awkwardly with a crutch. He is often the subject of gossip and cruel taunting by the older boys. On one singular school day Sara’s life would change forever. Nazi troops arrive at her school with the intention of identifying and removing just the Jewish students. Terrified (there are perhaps a dozen), betrayed by other students, they try and escape. Unexpectedly, Sara is rescued by Julien who leads her through an underground tunnel out of the school to safety. He then explains that she must hide in an old barn on his parents’ property. Julien’s act is extraordinary (supported by his mother), considering the risk involved; the Nazis were lethally unforgiving to anyone assisting the Jews. And thus begins the essence of the narrative: Sara will spend a harrowing year hidden in the barn with Julien as her only contact with the outside world. Their friendship slowly evolves, and is Orlando Schwerdt and Ariella Glaser in White Bird the fulcrum of the story. White Bird is a remarkable film, and together with the film Wonder poses important questions about the courage required to choose kindness. White Bird. Directed by Marc Forster. articles.text: Wonder is a touching family film that focuses on a 10-year-old boy, Auggie (Jacob Tremblay), who since birth has suffered with a craniofacial genetic disorder, an affliction that has distorted his face (he has endured some 27 surgeries). For so many reasons this story is life-affirming and brims with a surprising humanity. Auggie has always been homeschooled by his mom, Isabel (Julia Roberts). But now he finds himself confronting leaving the safety and embrace of his home and family, which includes his father Nate (Owen Wilson) and his sister Via (Izabela Vidovic). He is about to begin his first year in middle school, a place where he will confront for the first time the judgment of his peers. As Isabel and Nate walk him to school, Isabel utters a quiet prayer, saying, “Please, don’t let the kids be cruel.” And yet she knows that by definition that cruelty can define so many aspects of middle school. So, Wonder is about how Auggie strives to adjust to an environment for which he is profoundly unprepared. But to this film’s credit, it is never overly sentimental or maudlin; rather it inserts into the story other points of view. An example would be Via, who for much of her life has felt on the periphery of the family, understanding intellectually why Auggie has required so much of her parents’ attention. articles.text: Piedmont journalist and author William Gee Wong will discuss his latest book, Sons of Chinatown, in a talk at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Thursday, February 6, at 7:00 p.m. Born in Oakland’s Chinatown and for many years a Piedmont resident, Bill Wong will present a riveting discussion with colleague Bruce Koon about Chinese American history during the Chinese Exclusion Era, centered around Wong’s recent book, Sons of Chinatown. The conversation will begin with a slide show followed by a discussion with Wong and Koon. There will be opportunities for questions from the audience. A reception will follow the talk. Requa and his wife Sarah developed “The Highlands,” an estate built around a house that overlooked Lake Merritt, the Bay, and the San Francisco Peninsula. “The Highlands” was among the first impressive houses to be built in Piedmont. The Highlands was on a knoll where the present Hazel Lane and Requa Road meet. The house had 22 bedrooms, an adjoining wing for domestic help, and 11 hired hands had other quarters on the estate. Since it was a long trip in horse-drawn vehicles to Oakland via Vernal Avenue (now Highland Avenue), Moraga Road, and Piedmont Avenue, The Highlands was all but self-sufficient. Requa died at home in 1908 at the age of 80 and in 1923 the mansion was demolished. Today’s Highland Avenue is named after Requa’s estate. It is interesting to note that Piedmont High School’s mascot is the “Highlander,” and the school colors, purple and white, were purported to have been Sarah Requa’s favorite colors. articles.text: Group strength and conditioning session at BodyFit Training Rockridge We are bombarded with fitness program ads this time of year. Strength training, fueled by recent advances in sports training and medicine, is a hot topic today, with gyms changing their marketing to get in on the buzz. Real strength training, however, is an intentional program that builds foundational stability and resilience in all movement planes and using all muscle types. Older modes of exercise, like cardio-driven HIIT (high-intensity interval training), optimize short term calorie burns, while strength training impacts are broader and last long beyond your workout. What is real strength training? A true strength program focuses on programatically stimulating muscle and nervous system adaptations to build overall strength and health. This systematic approach contrasts with random circuit training or “toning” workouts, which often use weights but focus on calorie burn or aesthetics. Real strength training has four key pillars: 1. Progressive Overload: Increasing the demands on your muscles over time by lifting heavier weights or improving efficiency. This principle drives muscle growth and neuromuscular efficiency. Lighter weights and high-rep workouts may improve endurance and tone, but don’t deliver the stimulus needed for gains in strength and stability. 2. Compound Movements: Full body exercises like squats, deadlifts, presses, and pullups engage multiple muscle groups, promoting overall strength and functional movement. These multi-joint exercises require coordination and core stability, unlike isolation movements often used in floor workouts or circuit training. Accessory movements are also used to help build mobility and strengthen the muscle groups. 3. Balance of Rest and Intensit y: Strength training involves lifting heavy weights (70–90% of one-rep max) with proper form. Rest periods between sets (1.5-3 minutes) allow recovery for maximum effort set to set. In contrast, circuit training prioritizes cardiovascular endurance by minimizing rest and focusing on heart rate zones. 4. Periodization and Recovery: Structured progressions balance load, intensity, and volume, ensuring steady improvements while preventing plateaus, overuse injuries, or boredom! Recovery—through rest days, sleep, and nutrition—is essential for muscle repair and growth. GOOD THROUGH FEBRUARY 2025 GOOD THROUGH FEBRUARY 2025

articles.text: Are you changing jobs soon? If so, you’ll obviously be interested in your new salary — but you’ll also want to look at other financial considerations. Here are some of the most important ones: • 401(k) If you had a 401(k) plan through your previous employer, you’ll need to decide what to do with it once you’ve joined a new employer. You could just cash it out, but you’d pay taxes and possible penalties. You could leave your 401(k) with your previous employer, if allowed, and if you have been happy with your plan’s performance. Or you could move your 401(k) into your new employer’s plan, which might be a good choice if the new plan has lower fees and attractive investment options. You’d also want to ask whether the new employer offers matching contributions. Finally, you could roll over your old 401(k) into a traditional IRA, which would give you more investment choices. • HSA/FSA If your new employer offers a health savings account (HSA) as part of a high-deductible health plan, you may want to take advantage of it. Your contributions are made with pre-tax dollars, your earnings generally grow tax deferred and your withdrawals are tax free, as long as they’re used for qualified medical expenses. Plus, you can carry unused funds through retirement, when you can still use them for qualified medical expenses. Your employer might also offer a flexible spending account (FSA), which can pay for a variety of health care costs, such as deductibles, co-payments and co-insurance. Generally, if you’re contributing to an HSA, you can’t fund an FSA in the same year, except for a limited purpose FSA. • Waiting period for health benefits You’ll want to ask your new employer if there’s a waiting eligibility period to enroll in its benefits plan — health insurance, dental, vision, and so on. If so, you may need to get COBRA coverage for a few months to stay in your old plan, unless you can be added to a spouse’s plan. When you go on your new employer’s health care plan, make sure you know what it covers. Depending on your situation, you might want to add supplemental health insurance. • Life insurance When you leave a job, your employer-sponsored life insurance will end, unless you have the option to convert your group term life policy into an individual permanent cash value policy. So, you’ll want to be sure your new employer offers at least the same insurance coverage as your old one. But you should also determine whether the group policy offered by your employer is sufficient for your needs. Depending on several factors, such as your income, spouse’s income and family size, you may need to supplement your employer’s policy with an individual term life insurance policy. • Other benefits Review your new employer’s benefits package carefully to see what’s available. Many employers offer tuition reimbursement for their employees, and some even provide college planning assistance for employees’ children. For example, your employer might offer matching contributions to a tax-advantaged 529 education saving plan, which can be used for college, some K-12 expenses and some trade/vocational school programs. Changing jobs can provide you with an opportunity to expand your career, learn new skills and broaden your social network. And it can certainly be financially rewarding, too — so make sure you know all the benefits involved. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. articles.text: As the Lighting Ceremony in Piedmont Park approaches each year, Piedmont residents are invited to send holiday greetings to their neighbors through donations to the Piedmont Beautification Foundation’s (PBF) Holiday Greeting Fund. This year, in addition to PBF’s regular funding initiatives, donors had the opportunity to support the reforestation of Dracena Park. PBF is delighted to report that the community responded with great generosity. Nearly $35,000 was raised in total, including $17,700 specifically designated for the reforestation project. Since July 1, PBF has also received more than $23,000 in donations for tributary trees and benches, given in honor of and in memory of Piedmont citizens. PBF extends its heartfelt thanks to all who contributed and is pleased to recognize the donors who supported the Holiday Greeting Fund, as well as those who made gifts since July 1. Special appreciation is also extended to the underwriters who financed the city-wide mailing, which invited everyone to participate in the newly expanded Piedmont Lights Up event. articles.text: Nancy Kent (left), Cathy Glazier, Patty Dunlap, Cameron Wolfe, Betsy Andersen, Tom Ramsey, Julia Burke, Jennifer Long, Nancy Bishop, Lorrel Plimier, Conna McCarthy, Rosanna Bayon Moore The Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) celebrated its 60th Anniversary at the City Council Meeting on January 21. President Patty Dunlap, along with other PBF Trustees and Advisors, presented Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen and the City Council with a $60,000 check in recognition of the milestone. The funds are designated for refreshing and enhancing many of the projects PBF has completed in partnership with the City over the past six decades. Mayor Andersen responded with a Proclamation expressing gratitude to PBF “for its vision, leadership, and generous partnership.” The Proclamation officially recognizes and celebrates the Foundation’s 60th Anniversary. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation was established in Spring 1964 when the Piedmont Garden Club proposed creating a trust with the City to ensure a permanent source of funds for beautifying parks, the Community Center, street plantings, and other civic improvements. The City Council embraced the idea, and on May 13, 1964, PBF was incorporated with eight Trustees: three appointed by the City and five by Piedmont Garden Club. The Foundation’s first President was Mrs. Herbert Dunn. A Legacy of Leadership Over the years, PBF has benefitted from a strong partnership with the City. Typically, the Mayor, Vice Mayor, and Chair of the Park Commission have been among the City-appointed Trustees. In total, 31 members of the Piedmont Garden Club have served as PBF President, supported by countless other club members who served as Trustees or Advisors. Many PBF leaders have also held key roles within the City. Currently, four former or sitting Mayors serve as Trustees or Advisors: Betsy Smegal Andersen, Jen Cavenaugh, Bob McBain, and Valerie Matzger. President Patty Dunlap is a past Chair of the Park Commission, and other Trustees and Advisors with ties to the City or schools include Tom Smegal, Susan Herrick, Nancy McHugh, Bobbe Stehr, Patty Siskind and Cameron Wolfe, Jr. ects throughout the City, including improvements to City Hall, Piedmont Park, the Tea House, the Hall Fenway, the Exedra Gates and surrounding area, the Linda, Kingston Triangle, the Ramona Triangle and installation of the Bufano Bears Sculpture in Crocker Park”. More recently, PBF has contributed to safety and sustainability initiatives, including one of the largest donations to the new swimming pool project, second only to that of PRFO. This donation will fund environmentally appropriate landscaping around the pool. Endowments for the Future PBF established its first Endowment Fund in 1991, with an initial gift from Winifred Brown Bell. PBF has worked hard to grow this fund substantially, safeguarding existing and future projects and ensuring funds during lean times. In 2017, a second Endowment Fund was created, thanks to gifts from John Bates, Jr. and Charles Bates, to provide ongoing maintenance for the City’s sports facilities. Impactful Projects As Mayor Andersen noted in her Proclamation, “PBF has successfully partnered with the City to complete scores of projHonoring Key Leaders No discussion of PBF history would be complete without nods to two of its most prolific Presidents, Barbara Magee and Jean Brown Wolfe. Both women served four years instead of the typical two and oversaw some of PBF’s most impactful projects. Their contributions are commemorated on City property: Barbara Magee at the Exedra overlook area and Jean Brown Wolfe at the garden surrounding the Tea House. A Year of Celebration To mark its 60th Anniversary, PBF has planned a series of events and activities. Over the next month, news articles will highlight PBF’s key projects, accompanied by games such as word finders, crosswords, and spelling bees. The Wednesday Walkers group will visit various PBF project sites over three weeks, and a walking map will be published to guide residents to these locations. President Patty Dunlap expressed her excitement: “We hope everyone will find a way to participate in the celebration of PBF’s 60 years and support our future endeavors.” PBF President Patty Dunlap (left) presents $60,000 check to Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen
